ta-l1d25q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 25. Lombard turns to 'person' as a name that admits numeral additions and is co-signified in the plural, asking whether, as it signifies essence in the singular, it does so in the plural. This seems to lead to two awkward results: if it signifies essence, 'several persons' means 'several essences'; if not, 'person' is equivocal between singular and plural. He gives arguments that it signifies essence in both numbers, from Augustine (what is common to the three is the essence) and from the question 'three what?', since 'what' asks about essence. He then reports and refutes a solution: 'three persons' means three having the common essence, which cannot account for Augustine's 'other in person'. His own solution is that 'person' in the plural with numeral terms signifies hypostasis ('three persons' as three hypostases). With partitive terms, 'another person' signifies hypostasis and 'other personally' signifies property, though each can signify both. He concludes that 'person' has a threefold sense in the Trinity. Four articles are announced: the definition of person; whether it is univocal of God and creatures; its commonness among the divine persons; and whether the three persons are three things or three beings.
claims: 'Person' in the plural with numeral terms signifies hypostasis; with 'personaliter' it signifies property.
'Person' has a threefold sense in the Trinity: essence, hypostasis, property.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e159.summary: The article sets out Boethius's definition, 'a person is an individual substance of rational nature', and gives the first argument that it is inadequate. A definition should be convertible with the defined, and personhood is found in God, angels, and humans, but Lombard (III, Dist. 10) says this definition does not fit the divine persons.
claims: Boethius's definition does not fit the divine persons.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e165.summary: Second argument. The parts of a definition correspond to parts of the thing, and the divine person is simple without parts.
claims: Definitional parts signify real parts.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e168.summary: Third argument. What is predicated of something directly should not be placed in its definition obliquely, and intellectual nature is predicated of a person directly (Socrates is an intellectual or rational nature), so 'of rational nature' is wrong.
claims: Nature is predicated directly of the person.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e175.summary: Fourth argument. A proper difference of a genus is not found outside it, and rational is a difference of animal, but persons are found in angels and God, who are not animals.
claims: 'Rational' is a difference of animal.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e178.summary: Fifth argument. In Boethius's and Cicero's scheme 'person' is coordinated with essence, subsistence, and substance, and in God nature and essence are the same, so 'of rational essence' would be better than 'of rational nature'.
claims: Natura and essentia are the same in God.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e181.summary: Sixth argument. Matter is the principle of individuation, and person is found where there is no matter, at least in God, so 'individual' should not be in the definition.
claims: Matter individuates.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e184.summary: Seventh argument. 'Substance' among Latins is equivocal between essence and hypostasis. If it stands for hypostasis, which is a particular substance, 'individual' is superfluous. If for essence, individuation, which in God is by distinction of property, would distinguish the essence, and since multiplying the defined multiplies the definition, several persons would be several essences.
claims: 'Substance' in the definition is either redundant or implies several essences.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e190.summary: Eighth argument. 'Person' is a name of substance, not of accident, since substance stands directly in its definition and Boethius separates person from accidents. But accidents are not placed in the definition of a substance, and 'individual' names an accident, since it signifies an intention, like genus and species, so it is wrongly placed as a difference of substance.
claims: 'Individual' names an intention, which is an accident.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e193.summary: Thomas's determination. As said earlier, 'person' taken in its commonness is not a name of an intention, like 'singular', 'genus', or 'species', but a name of a thing to which an intention belongs, the intention of the particular, in a determinate nature, intellectual or rational. So its definition contains three things: the genus of the thing signified ('substance'), the difference by which it is contracted to the determinate nature in which the person is ('of rational nature'), and something pertaining to the intention under which 'person' signifies its thing ('individual'), since it signifies rational substance not absolutely but with the intention of the particular understood.
claims: 'Person' names a thing to which the intention of particularity belongs, not an intention.
Boethius's definition gives the genus (substance), the contracting difference (rational nature), and the intention (individual).

ta-l1d25q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the first argument. The terms of the definition can be taken strictly by the propriety of the words, and then, as will appear, the definition does not fit the divine persons, as Lombard says; or broadly, and then it fits a person in any intellectual nature, as Boethius takes it, since he seeks the definition to show how there is one person in Christ, who has only the uncreated divine person.
claims: Taken broadly, Boethius's definition fits the divine persons.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the second argument. According to Avicenna a definition can be considered by what it signifies or by its intention. In the first way the definition and the defined signify the same (the Philosopher: the concept a name signifies is the definition), and what is placed directly in the definition is not part of the thing signified; if animal were part of man it could not be predicated of the whole, since no integral part is predicated of its whole. Man is not 'from' animal, rational, and mortal but is a rational mortal animal. The genus signifies the whole as undesignated, the difference as designating, and the definition and species as designated. So 'body' as part of animal differs from 'body' as genus (Avicenna): as part, it is a thing with three dimensions on condition that a further perfection, the soul, completes it, and is not predicated of animal; as genus, it is a thing with that nature from whatever form, signifying the whole indistinctly, while 'animate' designates the form. In composites genus and difference, though not parts, flow from parts, genus from matter and difference from form, so a composite definition shows real composition. In simple things, and especially in God, definitional composition reflects no real composition, only a conceptual one grounded in the truth of the thing, as if one defined God as 'divine intellectual substance': each name truly signifies God and their significations differ without real diversity. As the intellect states the being of a simple thing by affirmative composition of several names, it designates the quiddity of a simple thing by several names with a plurality of concepts but no diversity of thing. So the terms in the definition of a divine person are not simpler in reality than the person, only conceptually. Considered by its intention, the definition is not the defined but leads to knowledge of it, composed of intentions none of which is predicated of it, and this is only in the intellect that devises them; so there is nothing wrong in positing whole and part in God by the intellect's operation, as the subject of a proposition about God is part of the proposition.
claims: Genus and difference are not parts of the defined but signify the whole, undesignated or designating.
In God definitional composition is merely conceptual, grounded in reality, without real composition.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the third argument. Essence or nature can be signified as part (humanity), which cannot be predicated directly of the person, or as whole (man), which can. Here 'rational nature' is taken in the first way, as principle of the difference and not the difference, like rationality, which could stand in the definition of man only obliquely ('an animal having rationality'). In composites designated nature differs really from the person, since something is added to the nature, like designated matter, by which the common nature is individuated. In simple things, and especially in God, nothing is added in reality, so nature so signified differs from person only in mode of signifying, which is why it falls obliquely in the definition of a divine person.
claims: 'Rational nature' is taken as part, so it stands obliquely.
In God nature differs from person only in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e215.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Rational' is said strictly and properly when reason means a shadowing of intellectual nature, as Isaac says reason arises in the shadow of intelligence, since truth is not offered at once but found by discursive inquiry; so taken it is a difference of animal and does not fit God or angels. It is also taken commonly for any knowledge of a power not impressed in matter, and so it fits God, angels, and humans: Gregory calls an angel a rational animal, and Dionysius says the sensible and rational are in angels more eminently and counts reason among divine names. Boethius takes it this way.
claims: 'Rational' taken commonly as immaterial knowing fits God and angels.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e218.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. According to Boethius, in one sense nature is what informs each thing by its specific difference, so 'nature' names essence not absolutely but as determined to a genus or species. Since 'person' names a subsisting substance only in a determinate genus, intellectual nature, Boethius said 'nature' rather than 'essence'.
claims: 'Nature' names essence as determined to a kind.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e221.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. In individuation in composites, there is its cause, matter, which is not transferred to God, and its character, incommunicability, as something one and the same not divided among, predicated of, or divisible into many, which fits God. So Richard of St Victor put 'incommunicable' in place of 'individual'.
claims: Individuation's character is incommunicability, which fits God; its cause, matter, does not.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e225.summary: Reply to the seventh argument. 'Substance' is said four ways: as essence, found in all genera ('what is whiteness? colour'); as the individual in the genus of substance, first substance or hypostasis; as second substance; and as substance in common, abstracting from first and second. It is taken here in the fourth way and contracted by 'individual', as by a difference, to stand for first substance, as 'animal' in 'rational mortal animal' signifies the nature abstracted from species and is contracted by the difference. Some say substance stands for hypostasis: since a person has a threefold incommunicability, excluding universal community, the particular community of a part in a whole, and the assumable community of union with something nobler (human nature in Christ is not a person), 'hypostasis' excludes the first two and 'individual' the third. The first view is better, since this cannot be drawn from the meaning of the words, and the objection would remain about how 'substance' is taken in 'hypostasis is an individual substance'.
claims: 'Substance' in the definition is substance in common, contracted by 'individual' to first substance.
A person has threefold incommunicability: universal, as part, and as assumable.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e228.summary: Reply to the eighth argument. 'Person' names not an intention but the thing to which it belongs, so it names a substance, not an accident, and 'individual' is not a difference of substance, since the particular adds no difference to the species. The particular is made individual by an essential principle, matter in composites and the distinguishing relation in God, and because essential principles are unknown to us we often put something accidental in definitions to signify something essential, so the name 'individual', a name of an accident, designates the substantial principle of individuation. Other definitions are given: Richard of St Victor, correcting Boethius for the divine case, says 'a person is an incommunicable existence of divine nature', since 'rational', 'individual', and 'substance' do not properly fit God in common usage; the masters say 'a person is a hypostasis distinguished by a property pertaining to dignity'. These come to the same, but the masters' compares the person to the distinguishing property it underlies, Boethius's to the nature, and the person is related to both.
claims: 'Individual' is an accidental name used to signify the essential principle of individuation: matter in creatures, relation in God.
Richard's and the masters' definitions are equivalent to Boethius's, differing in what they relate the person to.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e246.summary: First argument that 'person' is said univocally of God and creatures. However different things are, they can agree univocally in a negation, as 'not being a stone' fits God and man, and personhood consists in a negation, since it is an individual (undivided) substance.
claims: Negations can be shared univocally.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e249.summary: Second argument. What is predicated by one name and one concept is univocal, and the name 'person' and its definition fit God and creatures (Boethius).
claims: One name and one definition imply univocity.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e252.summary: Third argument. Otherwise it is equivocal or analogical. Not equivocal, since the terms of the definition are not equivocal of God and creatures; not analogical, since nothing analogically said of God and creatures is prior in the creature, as 'person', transferred from creatures to God, would be.
claims: 'Person' is neither equivocal nor analogical.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e256.summary: Sed contra. Nothing is said univocally of things that do not share a most general genus, and God, not being in a genus, does not share genus, species, or accident with creatures, since he cannot be a subject (Boethius).
claims: God shares no genus with creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e259.summary: Second sed contra. 'Person' signifies something distinct in a nature, and the character of distinction differs: in God by relations of origin alone, in angels by absolute properties, in humans both ways (Richard).
claims: Modes of distinction differ in God, angels, and humans.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e262.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Person' is said of God and creatures neither univocally nor equivocally but by analogy. As to the thing signified it is prior in God, but as to the mode of signifying it is prior in creatures, as with all names said analogically of God and creatures.
claims: 'Person' is said of God and creatures analogically.
The thing signified is prior in God; the mode of signifying is prior in creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e265.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although 'individual' by its concept implies a negation, the negation is founded on something real, the distinction of a distinguishing principle, in which God and creatures are not univocal. Besides, the definition includes 'substance' and other terms that cannot be univocal, unless one held that 'person' names an accident, an intention, with substance in its definition as subject, like 'snub is a curved nose', which is against Boethius, who seeks the difference of person by dividing substance.
claims: The negation in 'individual' is grounded in a real distinguishing principle that differs in God and creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e268.summary: Reply to the second argument. According to the Philosopher nothing prevents some concepts from being non-univocal, so as the name 'person' is analogical, so is its definition.
claims: Definitions can be analogical.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e271.summary: Reply to the third argument. As to the thing signified 'person' is prior and truer in God, and in creatures analogically, but as to mode of signifying and imposition it fits creatures more familiarly.
claims: Priority in thing signified belongs to God; in imposition to creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e275.summary: The fourth argument, the sed contra that nothing is univocal of God and creatures, is granted.
claims: Nothing is univocal of God and creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e278.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The concept of person implies distinction in general, abstracting from each mode of distinction, so it can be one concept analogically in things distinguished differently.
claims: Person implies distinction in general, abstracting from its modes.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e290.summary: First argument that 'person' is not common in the Trinity. Whatever is common to the three signifies essence and is predicated singularly, like wisdom and goodness, and the persons are not distinguished in it, but 'person' is predicated plurally and the Father and Son are distinguished in person.
claims: What is common is essential and singular.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e293.summary: Second argument. Whatever is common and belongs to the concept of several things is a universal, so if 'person' is common to Father and Son and not outside their concepts (otherwise it would be an accident), it would be a universal, which is not in God.
claims: The common within concepts is universal.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e296.summary: Third argument, against the reply that it is common conceptually, not really. Even in a universal there is not the numerically same concept, as the same humanity in different individuals, only the same conceptually, so this does not prevent it being a universal.
claims: Conceptual commonness is the universal's commonness.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e300.summary: Fourth argument. What of itself has the character of incommunicability cannot be common, since these are opposites, and person does.
claims: Incommunicability excludes commonness.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e303.summary: Sed contra from Augustine in the text.
claims: Augustine treats person as common.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e306.summary: Second sed contra. Nothing can be counted with another except in what is common to both.
claims: Counting requires commonness.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e309.summary: Thomas's determination. There are two kinds of commonness, of thing and of concept. Commonness of thing, where something numerically one belongs to many, is found in nature only in the divine persons, and in the Trinity only for the essence and what pertains to it: attributes, operations, negations, and essential relations. 'Person' is common in the Trinity by commonness of concept, variously explained. Some say it is common by negation, since 'individual' implies negation, and such commonness does not make a universal, but this is insufficient, since 'person' implies something positive too. Others say it is common by proportion, as a ruler in a city and a sailor in a ship, the Father and Son relating alike as subsisting to the divine nature; others by intention, as colour and animal agree in the intention of genus; these come to the same, since commonness of intentions is by proportion of common to proper. This does not suffice either, since 'person' names not just an intention or relation of a subsistent to a common nature, as 'supposit' or 'particular' do, but the thing to which the intention belongs; that commonness is how 'supposit' is common to the three. Beyond these, which are somehow included, there is a commonness of concept founded in reality, as the concept of animal is common to man and ass. Such concepts are either common (animal) or special (man). In God, since there is really relation, there is a common concept of relation, and since there is really paternity, a special concept of paternity, so relation is common to paternity and filiation as a common concept in special ones. Yet relation is not universal to them, since every universal has different being in its inferiors, while in God there is one being, the same being of relation in paternity and filiation, so a common concept in God is distinguished not by being but only by special concepts, and nothing one by special concept can be numerically multiplied in God. So 'person' in God signifies in common the concept of a distinct subsistent in such a nature, and 'Father' the relation of a subsistent distinct by a special concept, and likewise 'Son'. So 'person' is not common to Father and Son in reality, since there is not one person of both as there is one essence, but as what has a common concept is common to what has special and proper concepts in which they are distinguished; yet it is not universal, since it does not have different being in Father and Son.
claims: 'Person' is common in the Trinity by commonness of concept founded in reality, not commonness of thing.
Negation, proportion, and intention accounts are insufficient.
A common concept in God is not universal, since there is one being in the persons.
concepts: commonness of thing vs. of concept

ta-l1d25q1-d1e312.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Person' is not common by commonness of thing, as the essence is, so although it does not differ really from the essence, it does not signify in the manner of essence. When the Father is said to be distinguished from the Son in person, the distinction is not in the common concept of person but only in the special concept, the concept of Father.
claims: Persons are distinguished not in the common concept but in the special concepts.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e315.summary: Reply to the second argument. Strictly, 'person' is not of the concept of Father, since in God there is properly no definition, genus, or species. Setting that aside, even if it is of the concept of Father, it does not have different being in Father and Son, so it is common to them not as a universal but only conceptually.
claims: In God there is no proper definition, genus, or species.
'Person' is not universal, lacking diverse being in its inferiors.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e319.summary: This also answers the third argument.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e322.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Although what is a person is incommunicable, the intention of person can be common, as Socrates is incommunicable while the concept or intention of individual is common, and conversely the intention of genus is designated as particular when contracted to this genus. So the concept of person, though it does not name a particular intention, is common, since it implies a general, not special, character of distinction, as the vague individual ('some man') is in a way common, implying individuation in general and not this or that character of it.
claims: The incommunicable can fall under a common concept, as with the vague individual.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e335.summary: First argument that the three persons cannot be called three beings or three things. Whatever is predicated absolutely in God is predicated singularly of the three, and 'being' and 'thing' are said absolutely.
claims: Absolute names are singular in God.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e338.summary: Second argument. As there is one deity of Father and Son, so one being and one quiddity, which yield only one God, so for the same reason there are not three beings or three things, since 'being' is imposed from being (esse) and 'thing' from quiddity (Avicenna).
claims: 'Ens' is from esse and 'res' from quiddity, both one in God.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e341.summary: Third argument. Father and Son are distinguished only by relations, and relation, in the respect by which it distinguishes, posits nothing.
claims: Relation as respect posits nothing.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e345.summary: Fourth argument. Damascene says the three persons do not differ in reality but are distinguished by reason and cognition, and what is distinguished only by reason is not three things.
claims: Damascene: persons differ only by reason.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e348.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: the things to be enjoyed are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
claims: The persons are 'things' to be enjoyed.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e354.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever are really distinguished are several things, and the persons are really distinguished. As the character of wisdom is really in God, so is paternity, and as God is really wise by the real character of wisdom, he is really Father, so really related, so really distinct, since these follow one another per se.
claims: The persons are really distinct, as paternity is really in God.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e357.summary: Thomas's determination. According to Avicenna (Dist. 2), 'being' and 'thing' differ as the two aspects of a thing: its quiddity and concept, from which 'thing' is taken, and its being. Since a quiddity can have being in the singular outside the soul and in the soul as apprehended, 'thing' relates to both: in the soul as res is from 'reor' (to think), outside the soul as something established and firm in nature. 'Being' is taken from esse, and since the three persons have one and the same being, 'being' taken substantively cannot be predicated plurally of them, since its form is not multiplied; taken participially and adjectivally it can, since such terms take number from supposits, not from the form signified (Dist. 22). The quiddity or form from which 'thing' is taken in God is twofold: absolute (essence, deity), which is not multiplied, so 'thing' from it is predicated singularly (Father and Son are one thing); and relative (paternity), which is other than filiation not only in the intellect but outside it. So from this relation 'thing' is predicated plurally, and the Father, Son, and Spirit are three things, not only in the soul but outside it, having firmness in nature.
claims: 'Being' taken substantively is singular in God, since there is one esse; taken adjectivally it can be plural.
'Thing' is singular from the absolute form and plural from the relative forms, so the persons are three things in reality.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e360.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Being' is in no way taken from a relation but from being, which is simply absolute in God, so it is predicated plurally not by its form but by its supposits, as an adjective or participle. 'Thing' is imposed from a quiddity or form that can be absolute or relative, so it can be predicated plurally though it is not referred to another by its name, since being absolute or relative is incidental to the concept of thing, as being rational or irrational is incidental to animal.
claims: 'Res' is indifferent to absolute and relative, so it can be plural.
concepts: res indifferent to absolute and relative

ta-l1d25q1-d1e363.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though there is one being as there is one deity, 'being' is an adjective and 'God' a substantive, so the cases differ. If quiddity means not only the absolute nature but the concept of any substance, accident, or relation, then though there is one absolute quiddity in God, there are several concepts of real relations, and so in a way several quiddities, though this cannot properly be granted, since quiddity, essence, and definition belong simply only to substances (the Philosopher). That is why 'thing' can be predicated both plurally and singularly.
claims: There are several concepts of real relations, in a way several quiddities, though not properly.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e367.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although relation by that respect does not posit something absolute, it posits the character of relation really existing in God, so it can be called a thing, and several opposed relations several things.
claims: Relations really existing in God are things.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e370.summary: Reply to Damascene, answered earlier (Dist. 2), where 'reason' is glossed as 'relation', called reason by comparison with the essence.
claims: Damascene's 'ratio' means relation.

ta-l1d25q1-d1e379.summary: An expositio textus. (1) The opinion that 'person' signifies essence is erroneous: if person and essence signified the same in both mode and thing, then as we say three persons we would have to say three essences, or deny both, and 'three having the common person' could equally gloss 'three essences'. It cannot be excused by the heretics' pressure, since no necessity forces granting what is false, and the usage should have ceased with the necessity. (2) That the plural was introduced by necessity seems empty, since the plural is the doubled singular, but by the concept of the name it signifies hypostasis in both numbers, and because hypostasis and essence are really identical in God, 'person' can stand for essence in the singular but not in the plural, which conflicts with unity of essence, so Lombard's distinction concerns usage more than signification. (3) The three persons are 'one essence' by real identity and 'of the same essence' by conceptual difference, but not 'from one essence', since 'ex' denotes efficient or material cause, while the genitive can denote any cause, and essence relates to person as formal cause. (4) 'Person' taken for property is not by proper signification but by real identity of distinguishing property and distinct person; 'another person' or 'several persons' signifies the person as numbered and distinct, fitting hypostasis, while 'other in person' signifies the character of distinction, fitting property. (5) There is no grade in the Trinity, since grade implies an order of dignity above and below (the Gloss on Exod. 20:26 condemns ascending by steps to make the Son less and the Father greater); Augustine takes 'grade' broadly for order, as 'cause' for principle, and 'subauthority' is not ascribed to the Son by the saints and seems improper.
claims: 'Person' does not signify essence in the plural; it signifies hypostasis in both numbers but can stand for essence in the singular by real identity.
The persons are 'of one essence', not 'from one essence', since essence is a formal cause.
There is no grade of dignity in the Trinity, only order.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 25 divides Lombard's treatment of what 'person' signifies in the plural: he refutes the view that it signifies essence and holds that with numeral terms it signifies hypostasis and with 'personaliter' property, concluding to a threefold sense. It announces four articles: the definition of person, univocity between God and creatures, commonness among the divine persons, and whether the persons are three things or three beings.
claims: 'Person' in the plural signifies hypostasis.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e151.summary: Article 1 defends Boethius's definition of person, 'an individual substance of rational nature'. 'Person' names a thing to which the intention of particularity belongs, so its definition gives the genus (substance in common, contracted to first substance), the determinate nature (rational nature, placed obliquely as part), and the intention (individual). Taken broadly the definition fits the divine persons: in God definitional composition is merely conceptual; 'rational' means immaterial knowing in general; 'nature' names essence as determined to a kind; and individuation means incommunicability, its principle in God being the distinguishing relation. Richard's 'incommunicable existence' and the masters' 'hypostasis distinguished by a property of dignity' come to the same.
claims: Boethius's definition, taken broadly, fits the divine persons.
Individuation in God is incommunicability, whose principle is the distinguishing relation.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e238.summary: Article 2 holds that 'person' is said of God and creatures analogically, prior in God as to the thing signified and in creatures as to the mode of signifying and imposition. The negation in 'individual' is grounded in a real distinguishing principle that differs in God and creatures, definitions can be analogical, and 'person' implies distinction in general, abstracting from its modes.
claims: 'Person' is analogical between God and creatures.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e282.summary: Article 3 holds that 'person' is common in the Trinity not by commonness of thing, as the essence is, but by a commonness of concept founded in reality, as relation is common to paternity and filiation. Accounts by negation, proportion, or intention are insufficient. This common concept is not a universal, since a universal has diverse being in its inferiors, while the persons have one being. The persons are distinguished by their special concepts, and the incommunicable can fall under a common concept, like the vague individual.
claims: 'Person' is common by a concept founded in reality, not by real commonness.
It is not a universal, because the persons share one being.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e327.summary: Article 4 holds, following Avicenna's distinction of 'thing' from quiddity and 'being' from esse, that 'being' taken substantively is singular in God because the three have one being, though adjectivally it can be plural. 'Thing' is singular from the absolute form (essence) and plural from the relative forms, so the persons are three things really, not only in the soul. Relations really existing in God are things, and Damascene's 'reason' means relation.
claims: The persons are three things, but not three beings in the substantive sense.
'Res' is indifferent to absolute and relative forms.

ta-l1d25q1-Dd1e374.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 25 rejects the view that 'person' signifies essence in the plural. 'Person' signifies hypostasis in both numbers but can stand for essence in the singular by real identity. The persons are 'of one essence', not 'from one essence', since essence is formal cause. 'Person' is used for property by real identity, and there is no grade of dignity in the Trinity, only order.
claims: 'Person' signifies hypostasis; the persons are of one essence; no grade in God.

ta-l1d25q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 25 treats the name 'person'. Article 1 defends Boethius's definition, 'individual substance of rational nature', broadly taken, explaining its genus, nature, and intention and showing that in God definitional composition is conceptual and individuation is incommunicability grounded in relation. Article 2 holds that 'person' is analogical between God and creatures. Article 3 holds that 'person' is common in the Trinity by a commonness of concept founded in reality, which is not a universal since the persons share one being. Article 4 holds that the persons are three things, from the plurality of relative forms, but not three beings substantively, since they have one esse.
claims: Boethius's definition, broadly taken, applies to the divine persons.
'Person' is analogical between God and creatures and common in the Trinity by concept, not as a universal.
The three persons are three things but one being.
